body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
Part 8 of #33160, follow-up of #34561.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
#34561 introduced the `solver="newton-cd"` which uses coordinate descent without gram matrix (=Hessian), i.e. like `ElasticNet(precompute=False).` It only uses the full hessian implicitly. This works by **taking the square root** of the Hessian (X'WX) and formulating the update step (one Newton iteration) as a least squares problem with penalty.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This does not work out of the box for the multinomial/multiclass setting because the pointwise hessian (W) is not diagonal.
> Several attempts of approximations that e.g. glmnet uses don't converge on simple problems.

This PR extends #34561 by introducing a dedicated coordinate descent solver for the multinomial. It uses an analytic LDL decomposition of the pointwise hessian (aka covariance of the multinomial) in order to take the square root of X'WX.

This is a very good solver for `n_features > n_samples`, thus closing this gap in solver options (currently only saga, but it often has convergence issues).

title: PERF: Speed up kdtree when distance metric's p is 1 or 2
body:
While poking around at a profile output for the example referenced in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/25812 I noticed that `pow()` was using a lot of time.

Since the exponent is usually `dist_metric.p`, which is in most is cases 1 or 2, this allows for a fast path to skip the overhead of calling `pow`. INF case is already bypassed by these codepaths.

Thus, the only case which is getting more overhead is when it's `1 / dist_metric.p` and `p` is 2, and `MinkowskiDistance` which can accept arbitrary positive floats for `p`.


#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
No need to call `pow()` when exponent is 1 or 2.

title: Possible performance improvements for kd-tree or ball-tree with multi-threading at fit time
body:
As reported here: https://skops.readthedocs.io/en/latest/auto_examples/plot_intelex.html

For small `n_features`, `KNeighborsClassifier` uses either BallTree of KD-tree algorithms. At this time, scikit-learn builds this tree sequentially.

We could recursively build the branches in parallel using a `ThreadPoolExecutor` instance and call submit for each children of a given node. Note that each node splitting operation (starting from the root) is one Cython function call that releases the GIL, so using thread-based parallelism should be efficient.

The second speed-up reported in plot_intelex.html above (at inference time) is mostly linked to the fact that scikit-learn `KNeighborsClassifier` does not enable parallel neighbors queries with the default value of `n_jobs` when using the kd-tree or ball-tree algorithms.

From a user's point of view, this is not ideal either: when using the brute-force algorithm, we rely on OpenMP and automatically use as many threads as CPUs available.

title: FIX respect copy=False in mutual_info_regression for target array y
body:
### Description
This PR fixes a bug in `mutual_info_regression` where the target array `y` was always copied, regardless of the `copy` parameter value. 

While the feature matrix `X` respected the `copy=False` parameter, `y` was always copied because `scale(y, with_mean=False)` was called without passing the `copy` parameter (which defaults to `True`), and `y` was not cast with `copy=copy`.

### Proposed Changes
- Inside `_estimate_mi` in `sklearn/feature_selection/_mutual_info.py`:
  - Cast `y` using `y = y.astype(np.float64, copy=copy)`.
  - Perform scaling in-place with `y = scale(y, with_mean=False, copy=False)`.
- Added `test_mutual_info_regression_copy` in `sklearn/feature_selection/tests/test_mutual_info.py` to verify that:
  - Setting `copy=True` leaves the original arrays unmodified.
  - Setting `copy=False` modifies the original arrays in-place.

Fixes #28793

**Note:** Together with #32659, the way to specify penalties is then 100% aligned with 
- `SGDClassifier(alpha=.., loss="log_loss")` (this is even the identical model!)
- `ElasticNet(alpha=.., l1_ratio=..)`
- `Lasso(alpha=)`
- `PoissonRegressor(alpha=)`

All use `1/(2n) * sum(deviance loss) + alpha/2 * ||w||_2`. See #15657 for further reasons of this choice.

For historians, the parameter `scale_C` which devided `C` by `n_samples` was once deprecated in #821.

<details>

**NOTE:** This is outdated content.

#### Open questions
1. Default `alpha`
   While the future default is currently `alpha=1`, a much smaller value might be better in practice, e.g. alpha=1e-4. Tiny regularization is also the main effect of `C=1` as it scales the penalty by 1/n_samples.

   For optimal prediction $p=P(Y|X)$, the expected log loss is the Shannon entropy (up to a factor) $E[log loss] = H(p) = -p \log(p) - (1-p)\log(1-p)$. The maximum is achieved at p=0.5 with H=0.69, some more values: H(1e-3) = 0.007, H(1e-6) = 1.5e-5. This shows, that `alpha=1` is a pretty strong penalty (for features of scale 1 or smaller).

2. Depending on the default of `alpha`, a good default for `StackingClassifier(final_estimator=..)` is basically no or tiny regularization.

</details>

This will be a highly controversial issue, therefore a lot of fun ahead 🎉

**Outdated content**
**The main reason for this change is that the current API is objectively bad design.** ~~Currently, I need to specify 3 parameters (`penalty`, `C`, `l1_ratio`) for just 2 effective parameters (the L1 and L2 penalization). On top, it warns a lot when mixing those, e.g. `penalty="l2"` and `l1_ratio=0`, but why on earth...~~

</details>

#### More arguments for `alpha` instead of `C`
1. API consistency: LogisticRegression is the only linear model using an anti-penalty `C`, all the others use penalty `alpha`, see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/28711#issuecomment-2030156413.
4. Literature:
  - The invention of using a Ridge penalty with logistic regression, https://www.jstor.org/stable/2347628 (Cessie et al 1992), uses a penalty (like `alpha`) and not an anti-penalty (like `C`). The papers for Lasso & Elastic-Net in combination with logreg do the same (use penalty like `alpha`).
  - I have a hard time (=I did not succeed) to find any (famous) ML book like ESL using the anti-penalty.
5. Other reference packages: The most famous R package glmnet (and others) uses a penalty (like `alpha`, they call it `lambda`, but that does not work in Python) and not an anti-penalty (like `C`).
6. Point of view of optimization: the penalty (like `alpha`) version can be seen as regularization to prevent singular behaviour (analogous to Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm), see Nocedal.
7. Original decision and discussion: I cannot find any discussion about the original introduction of `C` vs. `alpha` in LogisticRegression in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/commit/2993becc3dde6c15b11e0f79a05dc8bc022fd9cb. My guess is that liblinear's parameter names were just inherited.
8. Practicality: One never needs `C=0` (`alpha=np.inf`), but `C=np.inf` (`alpha=0`) is used very often. Zero is a much better defined value than infinity.
9. `C` interferes with class weights. Higher class weights means less regularization.
10. The main reason for `C` (and IFAIC its origin) is the analogy with support vector machines. SVM were once very powerful, but have become less and less important in practice. My prediction: this trend will continue.

#### Study of possible default values for the penalty
See https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/32042#issuecomment-4366344257 and the linked notebook https://github.com/lorentzenchr/notebooks/blob/master/logistic_regression_optimal_penalty.ipynb.

title: PRF Mitigation heuristics for HGB scalability
body:
Finally, I have something that has a uniformly positive impact on the 8 scenarios I'm testing:
- Big machine with default OMP settings
- Big machine with `OMP_PROC_BIND=close` (avoids penalizing runs that use fewer threads than what's available on the machine)
- Laptop with active wait disabled (the default behavior of conda-forge packages)
- Laptop with active wait enabled

(× libgomp & libomp for each of those)

And it can be very/hugely beneficial in some scenarios (2-10x speed-ups):
- small to medium datasets on a big machine
- small to medium-big datasets on laptops with active wait disabled

#### Reference Issues/PRs

Implements item 4 (partially), item 5 and item 6 of https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34764#issuecomment-5343004000

I'd also say it closes #14306, though that issue does have some ideas that aren't implemented here, in particular parallelizing over blocks of samples × features when building histograms. Benchmarks show HGB does keep scaling up to 16-32 threads for many medium/big datasets, as long as active wait is enabled, which I'd personally consider good enough for now.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

- Detect whether the OpenMP runtime uses active wait, i.e. whether idle threads spin instead of sleeping while waiting for work (`_openmp_uses_active_wait` in `sklearn/utils/_openmp_helpers.pyx`). This is done by parsing the environment dump the runtime prints under `OMP_DISPLAY_ENV=VERBOSE`, in a short-lived subprocess. Active wait makes rejoining a parallel region much cheaper, so all the heuristics below branch on it.
- Cap the number of threads used to grow each tree, based on the number of features and samples (`BaseHistGradientBoosting._get_heurirstic_optimal_n_threads`), instead of always using every available thread.
- Same idea for binning: `_BinMapper`'s `n_threads` parameter is renamed to `max_n_threads` since it's now only an upper bound, the actual thread count used being derived from the amount of data to bin.
- In `Splitter.split_indices`, fall back to a single-threaded partitioning pass when there isn't enough work per thread to justify the chunking/offset bookkeeping of the multi-threaded version.
- In `Splitter.find_node_split`, when active wait is disabled, skip parallelizing over features when there are too few of them relative to `n_threads`.

#### AI usage disclosure

Mostly not, except for the active wait detection: Claude helped find a way to make the subprocess-based `_openmp_uses_active_wait` fast enough not to matter (result cached after the first call, subprocess kept minimal to avoid a full `import sklearn`).

https://pr-81.sklbench-dashboard-preview.pages.dev/

title: Testing functionality to catch thread-safety issues, and a fix for one problem it finds

labels.name: free-threading

labels.name: Parallelism and scalability
labels.description: All things related to efficient handling of cores via thread-based or process-based parallelism.

body:
#### Background

I am working for Quansight on a contract to improve free-threading/threading support in Scikit-Learn.

To ensure thread-safety, it's useful to have test infrastructure that will provide:

* A way to identify thread-safety issues in code that has previously mostly been run in process pools. Free-threading's lack of GIL makes thread safety issues more likely than in the past.
* A way to prevent _future changes_ to the code introducing new thread-safety problems.

A good starting point here is focusing on operations that are _already_ parallel, where users might reasonably expect to be able to turn threading on as a `joblib` backend and have it Just Work. These operations also work in a very particular way: create some tasks, run them in a worker pool, get back the results of the tasks.

What can go wrong in this particular idiom? Switching from a process pool to a thread pool introduces thread-safety issues with the _inputs_ to a `Parallel()` operation: whereas mutating in a process is fine, mutating in a thread can affect other threads, or future interactions with the object in the main thread.

This suggests a starting point for a invariant to be using in testing: **the inputs to a `Parallel()` operation that can correctly run with both process and thread pools should not change when the function is run.**

> **Note:** `pytest-run-parallel` won't catch these sort of problems, as the problem here is not with shared global state, but with shared temporary and/or internal state.

#### What this PR does

When `pytest` is run with a new `--thread-safety-testing` flag:

1. `Parallel()` switches to running using a thread pool.
2. Arguments passed to functions called in parallel are tracked to see if they changed as part of execution. "Change" is calculated heuristically, with a hash.

This testing mechanism causes many tests to fail, suggesting objects are being mutated in the thread pool. At least in some cases this would suggest data races.

To demonstrate one of the (potential) problems it identifies, I fixed a real problem it identified: in `BinaryTree`/`KDTree`, certain C-level attributes were being modified in a non-thread-safe way. In normal Python with a GIL this was _maybe_ safe, depending where the GIL was released. In free-threaded code this is definitely not safe.

In practice these attributes weren't actually used by sklearn, so this wouldn't have impacted users, and removing them altogether seemed the easiest way to solve the problem.

In the short term I will keep going through the identified problems to see if there are any that impact real-world usage. title: FIX Avoid densifying sparse columns in QuantileTransformer/RobustScaler quantile computation
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #34298. Fixes #34857.

Supersedes #34451, which proposes the same `_sparse_column_percentile`-style fix for #34298 but without the part fixing #34857. Credited @Stag51 as co-author on the commit implementing it and in the changelog.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

Two related bugs in how `QuantileTransformer` (and `RobustScaler`) compute quantiles from sparse columns:

- #34298: with `ignore_implicit_zeros=False`, computing the quantiles densified the column into an `n_samples`-sized array, which can be very slow or OOM for extremely sparse matrices.
- #34857: when a column hit the subsampling path, only `subsample * len(column_nnz_data) // n_samples` non-zero values were kept, this can round down to a handful of points, so large chunks of the output distribution collapse to a single value.

To fix #34298, I added `_sparse_column_quantile`, which computes `nanquantile`-equivalent results directly from the non-zero data plus an implicit-zero count, without ever densifying the column.

I also ported the same fix to `RobustScaler`, which had the identical densify-then-`nanpercentile` pattern.

For #34857, the subsampling path now draws up to `self.subsample` non-zero values directly and subsamples the implicit-zero count proportionally instead => The amount of real signal retained no longer depends on how sparse the column is relative to `n_samples`. But the calculation volume is limited to O(`self.subsample`) which is the purpose of this parameter.

title: CPU oversaturation/oversubscription due to third-party libraries when running containers on Linux

labels.name: Needs Triage

body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Background

This is the result of a discussion with @ogrisel and @jeremiedbb, fleshed out and with some additional ideas. I make my suggestion at the end, but will require feedback before I do any of the work.

### The problem

When using a container on Linux (Docker, Kubernetes, anything using cgroups), you can set a CPU quota, something like "this process gets 2 cores worth of compute."

Unfortunately, not all third-party C libraries know this. At minimum OpenBLAS does not seem to know about this limit (). So if you have 64 core machine, and run a Kubernetes pod with 8 cores, and OpenBLAS will think it has 64 cores, and it will be much much slower. Similarly libgomp and libomp. MKL builds on OpenMP so maybe no point in filing there until libgomp/libomp are fixed.

* https://github.com/OpenMathLib/OpenBLAS/issues/6059
* https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=127651
* https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/225493

This is a performance problem for scikit-lean users.

### Demonstration

My CPU has 12 cores. I set up a cgroup with equivalent of 2 cores, but OpenBLAS still reports 12 cores:

```
$ systemd-run --user --scope --property CPUQuota="200%" -- python -c "import threadpoolctl; import numpy; print(threadpoolctl.ThreadpoolController().lib_controllers[0].get_num_threads())"
12
```

### Potential fixes

I am going to be fixing one case as a side-effect of https://github.com/joblib/joblib/issues/1846: when using `joblib.Parallel`, the number of cores will be constrained using `threadpoolctl`, including in sequential cases. However, this is a strange fix where if you don't use `joblib`, you still have the same performance problem.

So what else can be done until OpenBLAS any other relevant libraries fix this issue?

#### Option 1: joblib or scikit-learn set the limit correctly, on import

Instead of doing this in `Parallel` in the sequential case, do it on import of `joblib` or maybe `sklearn`: `threadpoolctl.threadpool_limits(limits=joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1))`.  (Technically this won't fix the above example because of https://github.com/joblib/loky/issues/634 but it will work in Docker or Kubernetes, and everywhere once that issue is fixed).

Pros:

* Fixes the limit for all use cases.

Cons:

* Importing a library changing global configuration. This is not very nice.

#### Option 2: sklearn sets the limit whenever calling into OpenMP or OpenBLAS

Pros:

* If you do `with threadpoolctl.threadpool_limits(limits=joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1))` it undoes the limits when done, so it's not a _permanent_ global config change, it's just DTRT.

Cons:

* This adds performance overhead of all these calls.
* Lots of code changes.

#### Option 3: Documentation of the problem and how to solve it

Pros:

* No impacts on global behavior.

Cons:

* Most people won't notice the documentation.
* If the situation improves or changes, most people won't re-read the updated docs.

#### Option 4: Warn on import

If `os.process_cpu_count() > joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1)` then that means cgroups is restricting CPU count further, so warn the user and tell them what to do. In practice should probably also docs to explain in more detail.

Pros:

* More likely to be noticed than docs.

Cons:

* Users will still have to do work.

### My suggestion

After further thought, I think setting the limit on import (option 1) is actually reasonable. The hope is that this is a stop-gap and can eventually be removed once the relevant libraries DTRT, and in practice for the vast majority of people this is the right thing to do.

If that's not acceptable, docs + warning is what I would suggest doing.

I can proceed with either, once there is some consensus.

### Introduce yourself

I'm an undergraduate economics student at UC Davis. I use scikit-learn for data analysis and use permutation importance to understand which features matter. This is my first issue filed against scikit-learn.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

**What:** When `max_samples` is set below 1, features that the model never uses still get non-zero permutation importances. By definition, shuffling a column the model does not look at cannot change the predictions, so its importance should be exactly 0. With `max_samples=1.0` the importance is indeed 0; the problem only appears when a subsample is used.

**My example:** The model only uses feature 0; features 1 and 2 are pure noise that the model never reads. With `max_samples=0.5`, both features 1 and 2 get an importance of −0.0104. The 5 repetitions (`n_repeats=5`) return exactly the same value, so the standard deviation is 0. The bias changes in magnitude and sign with the subsample size: −0.026 at 0.2 and +0.006 at 0.1. This shows it is sampling noise, not a real feature contribution.

**Cause** (I read `sklearn/inspection/_permutation_importance.py`): The baseline score is computed on all rows, while the shuffled score is computed on the subsampled rows only, and the two are subtracted. The difference therefore mixes in the gap between the full-data score and the subsample score, which has nothing to do with the feature. The docstring says a fresh sample is drawn for each repetition; in practice the subsample is drawn once per feature before the repetitions, and all features share the same random seed — so repeating does not average the bias away (std = 0), and every irrelevant feature gets the same bias.

**Impact on users:** `max_samples` exists to save time on large datasets. With this bug, irrelevant features get spuriously positive or negative importances, which can make them look useful or harmful, and can also corrupt feature ranking.

**AI usage disclosure:** I used an AI assistant to help identify this problem and write the reproduction script. The description above is my own, and the reproduction was run on my own computer.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np, sklearn
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
print(sklearn.__version__)
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
n = 200
X = rng.randn(n, 3)
y = 3 * X[:, 0] + rng.randn(n)          # only feature 0 matters
X[:, 1:] = rng.randn(n, 2)                # features 1, 2: pure noise
model = LinearRegression().fit(X[:, :1], y)  # model uses ONLY feature 0 ...
class OnlyFirst:                              # ... wrapped so it accepts 3 columns
    def fit(self, X, y): return self
    def predict(self, X): return model.predict(X[:, :1])
    def score(self, X, y): return r2_score(y, self.predict(X))
est = OnlyFirst()

r = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=0.5, random_state=0)
print("importances_mean (max_samples=0.5):", r.importances_mean)
print("importances (features 1,2 are ignored by the model, so must be exactly 0):")
print(r.importances[1:])

# Independent expectation: permuting a column the model never reads cannot change
# predictions, so the permuted score equals the score on the SAME rows -> importance 0.
r_full = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=1.0, random_state=0)
print("importances_mean (max_samples=1.0):", r_full.importances_mean)
print("baseline (all rows) r2:", r2_score(y, est.predict(X)))
for ms in (0.2, 0.1):
    r = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=ms, random_state=0)
    print(f"max_samples={ms}: importances_mean =", r.importances_mean, " importances_std =", r.importances_std)
```

### Expected Results

For every repetition, the importances of features 1 and 2 should be exactly 0 — identical to the result with `max_samples=1.0`.

body:
Fixes #35027.

title: FIX raise NotImplementedError for recursion PDP with categorical target features
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Follow-up from #33354, addresses https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33354#discussion_r3530561195

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

`BaseDecisionTree._compute_partial_dependence_recursion` passed grid values straight to `tree_.compute_partial_dependence`, which routes categorical splits by casting the raw feature value to a bitset index. But categorical values are ordinal-encoded by `_categorical_encoder` at fit time, and `predict`/`apply` re-encode through `_transform_categorical_features` before reaching the tree — the recursion path never did. It silently returned wrong values whenever the raw categories didn't already coincide with their `0..n_categories-1` encoding.

As discussed in review, supporting this properly isn't trivial (the grid would need to go through the fitted encoder), so for now let's just raise a `NotImplementedError` for categorical target features.

While looking into this, found that `HistGradientBoosting*` has a related but distinct bug: `_predictor.pyx::_compute_partial_dependence` (the recursion tree walker) has no categorical branch at all, and `grower.py` never sets `num_threshold` for categorical splits, so recursion silently used a `<= 0.0` split for any categorical target feature (not "correct by coincidence" like trees could be, just wrong). Applied the same fix there and parametrized the regression test over `DecisionTreeRegressor`, `HistGradientBoostingRegressor` and `HistGradientBoostingClassifier`.

I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation
- Test update
- Investigating the HGB bug

title: Add Accumulated local effects (ALE) to inspection

labels.name: Moderate
labels.description: Anything that requires some knowledge of conventions and best practices

body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I'd love to push the inspection module further by adding Accumulated local effects (ALE) from Apley 2020. A great description can be found in Christoph's online book https://christophm.github.io/interpretable-ml-book/ale.html

ALE fix the problem of partial dependence that they force the model to be evaluated on impossible or rare feature combinations. ALE are defined for numeric features that can be binned. From both bin edges, the slope of the partial dependence is calculated locally, i.e., only using observations in the bin. The slopes from all bins are cumsummed and vertically centered to the average response or prediction.

### Reference

Apley, Daniel W., and Jingyu Zhu. 2020. Visualizing the Effects of Predictor Variables in Black Box Supervised Learning Models. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology, 82 (4): 1059–1086. doi:10.1111/rssb.12377.

### Describe your proposed solution

Pseudo code to calculate ALE for one feature:

``` py
pd_slopes = np.zeros_like(bins)

for i, bin in enumerate(bins):
  X_bin = pick n_per_bin = 200 rows from data in bin
  if X_bin is empty:
    next
  pd = partial_dependence_brute(model, X_bin, grid = [lower bin edge, upper bin edge], sample_weights)
  pd_slopes[i] = pd[1] - pd[0]

return np.cumsum(pd_slopes)
```

title: Fix normalized BayesianRidge scores_ (#13852)
body:
Fixes #13852.

### Why

`BayesianRidge.scores_` includes the Gaussian likelihood constant but omits the normalization of its two Gamma priors. This makes the reported values incomplete, particularly when comparing different prior hyperparameters. The final score also needs to use the final fitted coefficients.

### Derivation

With `A = lambda I + alpha X.T X` and `mu = alpha A^{-1} X.T y`, completing the square and integrating out the coefficients gives

```
log p(y | X, alpha, lambda)
= 1/2 [p log(lambda) + n log(alpha) - log|A|
       - alpha ||y - X mu||^2 - lambda ||mu||^2 - n log(2 pi)].
```

The existing precision update equations correspond to Gamma priors with shape `alpha_1 + 1` and `lambda_1 + 1` and rates `alpha_2` and `lambda_2`. Thus each prior term `a log(t) - b t` also requires the constant `(a + 1) log(b) - log Gamma(a + 1)` when `b > 0`. At `b = 0`, the prior is improper, so the undefined constant remains omitted. The user guide gives the completed-square derivation, its equivalent covariance-space form, the derivatives, and the fixed-point updates.

### Changes

- Add the two Gamma normalization constants to `scores_` without changing the fitting updates or predictions.
- Evaluate the final score with the final fitted coefficients.
- Clarify the score API, private method name, and normalization caveats for fitted intercepts and sample weights.
- Compare initial and final scores against independent SciPy Gaussian and Gamma log densities for both `n > p` and `p > n`, including zero-rate priors.

### Verification

The 25 BayesianRidge-relevant tests in `sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_bayes.py` pass with the modified source module loaded against the installed scikit-learn 1.8 runtime. This source checkout lacks compiled extensions, so its native test invocation was unavailable. Ruff format and selected lint checks pass.

Hi, I'm Luis. I really like scikit-learn and wanted to start contributing to it. I looked for smaller issues I could understand and
solve carefully, with the hope of taking on more complex work as I get to know the codebase. This BayesianRidge issue caught my attention because it let me work through the mathematics and make a focused improvement.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`numpy.dtypes.StringDType` (and other new-style DType classes) crash `xp.isdtype()` across many sklearn utilities.

`numpy`'s (and array-api-compat's) `isdtype()` raises `TypeError` instead of returning `False` for numpy's new-style DType classes. sklearn calls `xp.isdtype(...)` in many places expecting `False` for unrecognized dtypes, not a crash.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
np.isdtype(np.dtypes.StringDType(), "numeric")
# TypeError: dtype argument must be a NumPy dtype, but it is a <class 'numpy.dtypes.StringDType'>.
```

```python
from sklearn.utils.multiclass import type_of_target
type_of_target(np.array(["a", "b", "a"], dtype=np.dtypes.StringDType()))
# TypeError: dtype argument must be a NumPy dtype, but it is a <class 'numpy.dtypes.StringDType'>.
```

Confirmed crash sites (14), all via `xp.isdtype()` except `unique_labels`:

| Function | File |
|---|---|
| `check_array` (any `dtype=`, incl. `None`) | `utils/validation.py` |
| `type_of_target` | `utils/multiclass.py` |
| `_is_integral_float` | `utils/multiclass.py` |
| `_assert_all_finite` | `utils/validation.py` |
| `_randomized_range_finder` | `utils/extmath.py` |
| `_safe_accumulator_op` | `utils/extmath.py` |
| `_find_matching_floating_dtype` | `utils/_array_api.py` |
| `_average` | `utils/_array_api.py` |
| `label_binarize` | `preprocessing/_label.py` |
| `LabelBinarizer.inverse_transform` | `preprocessing/_label.py` |
| `RidgeClassifier.fit` | `linear_model/_ridge.py` |
| `_encode` | `utils/_encode.py` |
| `_check_unknown` (→ `OrdinalEncoder.fit_transform`) | `utils/_encode.py` |
| `unique_labels` (`np.dtype(y.dtype, metadata=...)`) | `utils/_unique.py` |

Not affected: `is_multilabel`, `LabelEncoder.fit`, `_array_indexing`, `_determine_key_type`.

Related: #34383 (motivation — proposes `StringDType` internally in encoders), #9777 (same failure pattern, closed).

### Expected Results

Unrecognized dtypes should be treated like any other unsupported dtype (e.g. return `False`/`"unknown"`), not raise.

### Actual Results

`TypeError` at every site listed above (`unique_labels` raises via a different call, same root cause).

### Versions

```shell
Python 3.11.15
scikit-learn 1.8.0 and 1.9.1 (both confirmed broken)
numpy 2.4.4
pandas 3.0.2
polars 1.44.0
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

One internal helper, e.g. `_safe_isdtype()`, wrapping `xp.isdtype()` to catch `TypeError` and return `False`, used at all sites above instead of patching each individually.

title: In encoders, switch to faster string representation than `object` dtype
body:
Right now, `sklearn.preprocessing._encoders.BaseEncoder._check_X` has on its list of tasks "convert list of strings to object dtype". This is bad from a performance perspective, since:

1. You now have a pile of Python objects, and end up doing a lot of Python operations.
2. Interactions that involve missing data are extra expensive; I'm going to submit a separate issue/PR to speed one code path, but there may be others.

There are two superior alternatives available, that would allow bypassing Python altogether:

* NumPy's StringDType, with [custom support for missing data](https://numpy.org/devdocs/user/basics.strings.html#missing-data-support) - you can avoid using annoying nans, for example. Would require NumPy 2.0, but possibly a newer version if sklearn hits any bugs that were fixed in subsequent versions.
* Arrow string arrays, with Arrow's built-in support for missing data. Would require PyArrow, or some other Arrow library.

As an alternative to just switching completely internally, it would also be possible to add support for one, the other, or both in addition to object-based dtypes. Then users who have sufficiently new NumPy or PyArrow already installed would benefit from faster runtime, while still preserving backwards compatibility.

title: FIX Use exact expected path length in IsolationForest
body:
<!--
Thanks for contributing a pull request! Please make sure that your code passes
the tests. If your change is related to an open issue, please link it.
-->

#### Reference Issues/PRs

Closes #15724. Supersedes the stale #16721 (last updated Jan 2024), which took a lookup-table approach.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

`_average_path_length` used the Isolation Forest paper's logarithmic approximation of the harmonic number,

```
c(n) = 2 (ln(n - 1) + gamma) - 2 (n - 1) / n,
```

which is only accurate for large `n`. For small leaf sizes it is quite far off (about **30% too low at `n = 3`**, ~9% at `n = 5`, ~3% at `n = 10`), and this feeds directly into the anomaly scores through the path-length normalisation.

This PR replaces it with the **exact** expected path length

```
c(n) = 2 H(n - 1) - 2 (n - 1) / n = 2 (psi(n + 1) + gamma - 1),
```

where `H` is the harmonic number and `psi` the digamma function (`H(n) = psi(n + 1) + gamma`). It is computed with `scipy.special.digamma`, which is already used elsewhere in scikit-learn (`feature_selection._mutual_info`, `mixture._bayesian_mixture`), so no new dependency. The closed form is exact to machine precision and, as a bonus, subsumes the previous `n <= 1` and `n == 2` special cases into a single expression.

`_average_path_length` is computed once per tree at fit time and cached (`_average_path_length_per_tree`), so it is not on the per-sample scoring hot path and `digamma` has no meaningful performance cost here.

Accuracy after the change (exact vs the old approximation):

| n | exact | old approx | old error |
|---|-------|------------|-----------|
| 3 | 1.6667 | 1.2074 | 27.6% |
| 5 | 2.5667 | 2.3270 | 9.3% |
| 10 | 3.8579 | 3.7489 | 2.8% |
| 100 | 8.3748 | 8.3647 | 0.12% |

Impact on the anomaly score itself, from the issue: at `n = 3`, `E(h) = 1`, the score `s = -2**(-E(h)/c(n))` goes from `-0.563` (approx) to `-0.660` (exact), a ~15% difference.

#### AI usage disclosure
I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation
- Test/benchmark generation
- Documentation (the changelog entry)
- Research and understanding

I have reviewed and verified the changes.

#### Any other comments?

- `test_iforest_average_path_length` previously hard-coded the old approximation as its expected values, so it now (correctly) fails on `main`. I updated it to compare against an implementation-independent harmonic-number reference and added an explicit `n = 3 -> 5/3` assertion, which is the case the issue highlights (the old code returned ~1.207 there).
- `test_iforest_with_uniform_data` needed a small robustness change and I want to flag it explicitly. On perfectly uniform/degenerate training data no split is possible, so every leaf holds all `max_samples` samples and each point's path length equals the normalisation constant. Its anomaly score therefore sits **exactly** on the inlier/outlier decision boundary (`decision_function == 0`), and whether it rounds to a `+1` or `-1` label is decided by sub-ULP floating-point error. The old approximation happened to round to the inlier side; the exact value rounds one ULP (`2.2e-16`) the other way. Rather than depend on that coincidence, the test now asserts the meaningful invariant: degenerate data is never scored as a genuine anomaly (`decision_function >= 0` up to floating-point tolerance). Happy to adjust the framing if you'd prefer a different assertion.

title: DOC Correct the description of `tol` in the k-means estimators
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
Addresses the documentation half of #22519. Does not close it: that issue also
carries a proposal to *change* the convergence criterion, which is left open.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
`tol` is documented across the k-means estimators as:

> Relative tolerance with regards to Frobenius norm of the difference in the
> cluster centers of two consecutive iterations to declare convergence.

That sentence appears in five places and is inaccurate in all of them, in three
different ways. It also reads as if the normalisation were relative to the
centers themselves, which is what the reporter of #22519 originally expected.

**1. `KMeans` and `k_means` — scaled by the feature variance.**
`fit` sets `self._tol = _tolerance(X, self.tol)`, i.e. `mean(var(X, axis=0)) * tol`,
so convergence is declared when

```
(center_shift ** 2).sum() <= tol * mean(var(X, axis=0))
```

```
mean(var(X))        : 0.0839
_tolerance(X, 1e-4) : 8.39e-06     # actual threshold
mean(var(10*X))     : 8.388
_tolerance(10X,1e-4): 8.39e-04     # 100x larger
```

`MiniBatchKMeans` already documents this correctly ("a smoothed,
variance-normalized ... mean center squared position changes"), so `KMeans` was
inconsistent with its own sibling.

**2. `_kmeans_single_lloyd` / `_kmeans_single_elkan` — absolute.**
These are called with `tol=self._tol`, a value that has *already* been scaled,
so for them the threshold is absolute. Calling it "relative" is wrong in the
opposite direction.

**3. `BisectingKMeans` — absolute, unlike `KMeans`.**
It passes the raw `self.tol` to the inner k-means; `self._tol` is computed by
the inherited `_check_params_vs_input` but never used on that path:

```
user tol              : 0.0001
_tol (variance-scaled): 0.0820
tol passed to inner k-means: 0.0001      # raw value
```

So a `tol` that works for `KMeans` does not mean the same thing for
`BisectingKMeans`. This one surprised me, and it is the reason the wording is
not shared between the two classes.

This PR describes each of the three cases explicitly. Documentation only;
there is no behaviour change, and no changelog fragment since no behaviour
changed.

I deliberately scoped this to documentation. #22519 also contains a 2022
suggestion by @jeremiedbb to make the criterion a genuinely relative center
shift, with a deprecation cycle; that is a behaviour change and I did not want
to assume a four-year-old plan is still current, so I left it for a separate
discussion. Happy to adjust the wording, or to fold in the user guide if you
think `modules/clustering.rst` should say something too.

#### Introduce yourself
I use scikit-learn for general ML work. I came across #22519 while reading
around the k-means implementation and noticed the `tol` docstring didn't
match what the code actually does in any of the three cases described above.

title: Lasso(alpha) = SGDRegressor(alpha, penalty="l1"), but Ridge(alpha) = SGDRegressor(alpha / len(train_set))

labels.description: Issue resolution would not be easily handled by the usual deprecation cycle.

body:
### Describe the bug

`Ridge` and `SGDRegressor` are inconsistent in the way they handle the regularization hyperparameter `alpha`:

* `Ridge(alpha=alpha)` is equivalent to `SGDRegressor(alpha / m, penalty="l2", ...)`, where `m` is the training set size.
* But `Lasso(alpha=alpha)` is equivalent to `SGDRegressor(alpha, penalty="l1", ...)`, which is great.

Looking at the source code of `SGDRegressor`, it looks like `l1` and `l2` are consistent, so it must be a problem with `Ridge`. Perhaps it should be modified to divide `alpha` by `m`?

Is it just historical, or is there a rationale behind this?


### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso, Ridge, SGDRegressor

alpha = 0.1
m = 100

np.random.seed(42)
X = 2 * np.random.rand(m, 1)
y = 4 + 3 * X + np.random.randn(m, 1)

ridge = Ridge(alpha=alpha)
ridge.fit(X, y)
print("Ridge:", ridge.intercept_, ridge.coef_)

sgd_reg = SGDRegressor(
                       loss="squared_error", penalty="l2", alpha=alpha / m,
                       max_iter=10_000, tol=None, eta0=0.0001,
                       learning_rate="constant", random_state=42)
sgd_reg.fit(X, y.ravel())
print("SGDRegressor with l2:", sgd_reg.intercept_, sgd_reg.coef_)

lasso = Lasso(alpha=alpha)
lasso.fit(X, y)
print("Lasso:", lasso.intercept_, lasso.coef_)

sgd_reg = SGDRegressor(loss="squared_error", penalty="l1", alpha=alpha,
                       max_iter=10_000, tol=None, eta0=0.0001,
                       learning_rate="constant", random_state=42)
sgd_reg.fit(X, y.ravel())
print("SGDRegressor with l1:", sgd_reg.intercept_, sgd_reg.coef_)
```


### Expected Results

I would expect the `Ridge` model to be different from the `SGDRegressor` model, since it does not use the same `alpha` value. Instead, they are equal.

### Actual Results

But here is the output of the previous code:

```
Ridge: [4.22250784] [[2.76223165]]
SGDRegressor with l2: [4.22261191] [2.76235098]
Lasso: [4.48341837] [2.48477396]
SGDRegressor with l1: [4.4834874] [2.48492104]
```

As you can see, the `Ridge` model is equivalent to `SGDRegressor(alpha=alpha / m, ...)` instead of `SGDRegressor(alpha=alpha, ...)`. But `Lasso(alpha)` is equivalent to `SGDRegressor(alpha=alpha, penalty="l1", ...)`.

title: FIX prevent catastrophic cancellation in r_regression (#11395)
body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #11395.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

`r_regression` computes centered feature norms using a moment-based expression. Floating-point cancellation can make the mathematically non-negative centered sum of squares slightly negative for constant or near-constant columns, causing an invalid square root and propagating invalid correlations. This change clamps the intermediate squared norms to zero before `sqrt`, preserving existing results for active non-constant features and keeping dense, CSR, and CSC inputs consistent. Regression tests cover constant features, `force_finite=False`, sparse formats, high-magnitude cancellation, and active-feature preservation.

I am FinalSunFlower, contributing a numerically focused bug fix to scikit-learn's feature-selection utilities. I use scikit-learn for classical machine-learning workflows and was prompted by issue #11395 to improve the stability of `r_regression` on degenerate inputs.
